teaser: Every CVE makes me smile: moving to the client side took my servers out of the news, and the constraint turned out to be speed.
core_idea: Moving everything that can run in the browser to the client, with no database and no back end, leaves one upload server that stores only ciphertext, so a month of critical server vulnerabilities needs no response, and the same constraint makes building faster, leaner and more scalable; internal applications remain the growing risk, and every component should justify being on the server.

nodes.label: A month of critical server flaws
The attack surface you do not have
nodes.summary: Static files, the browser, one ciphertext store.

quotes.text: That is the best model: not responding faster to these things, but not having to worry about them at all.
Most of the time, in my experience, the honest answer is habit.

figures.caption: A month of critical vulnerabilities in server software, from 22 September to 21 October 2026: PHP, Plex Media Server, SiteGuard, Palo Alto PAN-OS, Cisco Secure Email Gateway, Ahsay, Ivanti Connect Secure, Zammad, Fortinet FortiMail, Citrix NetScaler and WordPress. My exposure to each: none.

The attack surface compared. A typical web product runs a web server and runtime, a framework and CMS, a database, admin panels and APIs, VPN and mail gateways, and file processing. These sites run static files, the reader's browser, and one upload server that stores ciphertext.

The constraint gives speed: 45 live sgit.ai sites, all static, in eleven weeks; 1,306 pages on this newsroom, with a meter and payments; 3 customers on customers.riskmandate.ai; and one server of our own, SG/Send, which stores only ciphertext.
